'''''Talinum paniculatum''''' is a [[succulent plant|succulent]] [[subshrub]] in the [[family (botany)|family]] [[Talinaceae]] that is [[native species|native]] to much of North and South America, and the Caribbean countries.<ref name=grin1>Under its current treatment as ''Talinum paniculatum'' (from its basionym ''Portulaca paniculata''), this species was published in ''De Fructibus et Seminibus Plantarum …'' 2:219. 1791. {{GRIN | accessdate=February 8, 2012}}</ref> It is commonly known as '''fameflower''',<ref name=grin1/> '''Jewels-of-Opar'''<ref name=grin1/> (a name borrowed from the title of the novel ''[[Tarzan and the Jewels of Opar]]'' by [[Edgar Rice Burroughs]]<ref>[http://msucares.com/news/print/sgnews/sg07/sg070628.html ''Jewels-of-Opar'', Mississippi State University]</ref>), or '''pink baby's-breath'''.<ref name=grin1/>

==Classification==
The species was described in 1760 under the basionym of ''Portulaca paniculata'' by [[Nicolaus Joseph von Jacquin]] (1727–1817), then recombined in the genus ''[[Talinum]]'' in 1791 by [[Joseph Gaertner]] (1732–1791). In current classification, ''Talinum paniculatum'' belongs to the family [[Talinaceae]], it was assigned in the past to the family of the [[purslane]] or [[Portulacaceae]].

==Appearance== 
''Talinum paniculatum'' bears [[tuberous root]]s<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Aflo8mKA0_gC |first=Maurizio |last=Sajeva |author2=Mariangela Costanzo  |title=Succulents: the Illustrated Dictionary |publisher=Timber Press |year=1997 |isbn=978-0-88192-398-8 |page=219}}</ref> and [[panicle]]s of [[flower]]s and produces tiny, jewel-like fruits. Its peculiarity is its very long root of orange colour that reaches about 80 centimeters. It is a very bad [[herb]] in [[crops]], and it proliferates very easily, since it roots very easily, even after it has been plucked and if it has any part of the root in contact with the soil. The plant as a whole can reach almost 2 meters high measured from the soil surface, where after maturity, its brown seeds (in abundance) spread easily through the surrounding area.<ref>Gaertn., 1791 In: Fruct. Sem. Pl. 2: 219, t. 128, f. 13</ref>

==Native range==
''Talinum paniculatum'' is native to the southern United States, much of [[Latin America]] (such as Paraguay and Uruguay) and the Caribbean. It has been introduced notably in Africa and Asia.<ref name=grin1/>

==Uses== 
''Talinum paniculatum'' is often grown as an [[ornamental plant]]. [[Cultivar]]s include 'Kingwood Gold',<ref name="Hodgson">{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/annualsforeveryp00larr |url-access=registration |first=Larry |last=Hodgson |title=Annuals for Every Purpose |publisher=Rodale |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-87596-824-7 |page=[https://archive.org/details/annualsforeveryp00larr/page/303 303]}}</ref> 'Limón',<ref>{{cite news |url=http://msucares.com/news/print/sgnews/sg07/sg070628.html |title=Limón talinum is jewel for gardens |first=Norman |last=Winter |work=Southern Gardening |publisher=Mississippi State University |date=2007-06-28}}</ref> and 'Variegatum'.<ref name="Hodgson"/>
The leaves are edible and have been used in [[traditional medicine]] in Asia.<ref name="tal">{{cite web |url=http://www.stuartxchange.org/Talinum.html |title=''Philippine Medicinal Plants'' Godofredo Umali-Stuart |year=2010 |accessdate=October 30, 2012}}</ref>

Used in home medicine as a [[diuretic]], healing, [[emollient]], vulval and anti-infective, it is also consumed in salads.<ref>Roskov Y., Kunze T., Orrell T., Abucay L., Paglinawan L., Culham A., Bailly N., Kirk P., Bourgoin T., Baillargeon G., Decock W., De Wever A., Didžiulis V. (ed) (2014). Species 2000 & ITIS Catalogue of Life: 2014 Annual Checklist.. Species 2000: Reading, UK.. Retrieved on 26 May 2014.</ref>
